5. Digging into the story, you can see why.

## 2. Avatar is the single most overrated movie of All time. Change ny mind.

**Score:** 331
**Body:** avatar is one of the most overrated movies ever made. Change my mind.

Visually? Incredible. Technically? Groundbreaking in 2009. But strip away the 3-D and Pandora scenery and you’re left with a painfully obvious story, cartoon villains and politics with absolutely zero subtlety. It's like if Tron in 1982 had a storyline attacking whatever was in style to attack back then. I dunno Acid rain? Ozone hole? World overpopulation?

Here’s the rreal reality:

The Story: It’s basically Dances With Wolves in space. Outsider meets natives. Outsider realizes his own people are evil. Outsider becomes better at being native than the natives. We’ve seen this story before.

The Politics: Cameron doesn’t even attempt balance. Corporation bad. Military bad. Natives good. Nature perfect. Western civilization guilty. The military commander isn't a character; he's basically a GI Joe villain created to make sure nobody accidentally sympathizes with humanity.

Jake’s Ridiculous Transformation: He learns an alien language while simultaneously mastering Na’vi hunting, culture, survival and animal riding in an absurdly short period. Learning another human language can take years. Jake basically speedrruns an alien civilization.

The Animals: Pandora's wildlife apparently doesn't experience pain whenever the screenplay needs an action scene. Animals can absolutely continue attacking after being injured, but repeated serious wounds usually affect behavior. Cameron's creatures routinely shrug it off because the scene isn't finished yet.

The Environmental Lecture: The Na’vi literally plug themselves into nature. Trees have memories. Animals are spiritually connected. Fine. But Cameron presents every bit of this as profound while making humanity almost comically corrupt.

And here's the funniest part: Cameron needed cutting-edge technology, hundreds of millions of corporate dollars and one of the world's biggest entertainment companies to make a movie warning us about technology, corporations and greed.

Then his anti-war message ends with a gigantic war sequence we're supposed to enjoy.

Again, Avatar isn't terrible as far as 2009 visuals. The spectacle itself is legitimately extraordinary for 2009.

But great visuals don't make a great story.

TL;DR: Avatar is a technological masterpiece attached to a recycled story, simplistic politics, convenient plot logic and villains drawn with crayons. Take away Pandora and the 3-D, and there's surprisingly little left.

Change my mind.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Thoughts on The Virgin Suicides (2000) dir. Sofia Coppola?

**Score:** 15
**Body:** First of all, the cinematography is amazing and it fits the dreaminess and the detachment of the movie so well that I don't think it'd be quite the same without it. The score by Air is invaluable to the movie's mood too, and within the broader music scene, I think it really set Air apart from their contemporaries.

I think the movie still holds up today in how it portrays societal indifference to teen illness and how troubled children are alienated. Seeing the events unfurl is particularly heart-breaking because of how contingent and preventable everything was. Indifference, fear, glamorization are all symptoms of the neighbourhood's passivity towards the plight of the girls. The adults turn blind eyes to them so as to label them as anomalies in a perfectly happy community, their peers alienate them because of their perceived "oddity", and the boys glamorize them for the sake of spinning their own tales of heroism where the girls are trophies to be rescued from their balconies through telescopes.

All these different forms of passivity push the girls towards fringes where they're observed instead of aided. The only instance of any "help", by the mother, is one that is warped and distorted with a desire to possess. I don't think it'd be a stretch to say Mrs. Lisbon urged for the girls to be locked so as to cut off any budding independence and keep them virgin, in a sense. She only allows the girls to be out insofar that the boys' intentions are "honourable" and that they're supervised by their father. The hard part is that her desires were right in that she wanted to protect the girls but crashed down on them akin to an avalanche of restriction.

Much can be said about all those who observe, but little can be said about the ones observed and that's the point of the film. It's easy to say that the girls ended their lives because of the sheer isolation as a rational explanation but that doesn't do their emotional headspace the justice it deserves, not in any way that can be done with words from the girls themselves. The boys do the girls wrong in completely shrouding them in mystery and untouchability, mythologizing five very human and feeling girls, but so do we as watchers when we reduce their actions as an "expected" and logically rooted, from our eyes, response to isolation. Albeit in a different way.

Suicide makes a person unknowable if they haven't left a paper trail to posthumously read through their inner state with. We, as observers, can only resort to explanations rooted in psychology to form some sense of a "Why?" and even writing and speech cannot sincerely capture the specific happenings in someone's head that lead them to it, whether it be for us or for the person themselves. It is the ultimate form of self-alienation given how completely it decimates any attempt of understanding or knowing.

I haven't watched a movie that crystallizes the unknowability of suicide so well as this film, and that's partly because of the little experience and taste I have with films so I'd love if anybody reading this could make similar recommendations! 

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I think this is maybe the definitive work on the male gaze. We are like the boys in the movie, trying to understand these girls without real insight into their lives. 

Everyone knows these girls are really going through it, but the boys are so entranced by their beauty and unknowability, they don’t really care about these girls’ emotional states or personal problems. 

This isn’t a straight indictment of the boys in the movie—they are developmentally less mature than the girls, have raging hormones, and have their own problems too. 

And the girls’ parents are so worried about puberty and their growing sexuality, they’d rather lock them inside. They, too, don’t care about these girls beyond their appearances. 

One thing I really love abt Coppola is how the movies *are* superficial—she works in a mode where the images tell her story, instead of relying heavily on dialogue to illuminate the internal lives of her characters. 

She’s made a lot of great stuff, but Virgin Suicides will always be my favorite. 
2. If you look at Sofia Coppola’s ouvre, she’s most interested in portraying girlhood and all of its ups and downs, but in this movie, she wants to show how it’s seen from the outside. We don’t get a lot of inside insight for the girls. The story is told from the outside. It’s all from the perspective of the neighborhood boys.

We never see exactly what the climate is, inside. Their parents are portrayed sympathetically, but always from a distance. We’re never shown a suppressive household from the inside. We never know exactly what the parents tell their daughters. We never know exactly why the girls felt so hopeless. There’s never an in-depth conversation between any of the sisters.

They function as a daydream, an urban myth. They’re never REAL people. It’s not important, in the context of the film, to know exactly what they felt, only that they are the doomed romantic heroines of our neighborhood boys' fantasies, early lessons in love and lust.

That’s why some people thought this was glamorizing suicide. They made suicide look good.
3. Nice write up. 

I thought about this for a while.  The only thing I can think of that was even in the ballpark of The Virgin Suicides was one of her other movies, Lost in Translation.   

I haven't seen her third film, The Beguiled, but that's probably what I'm doing tonight.

You might also like the novel that Virgin Suicides was based on.  I highly recommend it.  Same mood, but a deeper dive.  The audio book was phenomenal if that's your thing.
  - Her third is Marie Antoinette. 

The Beguiled is her 6th.

I prefer the former, but both are worth watching.
  - The Beguiled is awesome, I think it's about how feminine lust can eat itself alive. Women together, deprived of man, will make destructive decisions. They will destroy the man, even when they want the man so much. In many ways, it's the opposite of the Virgin Suicides.
4. The film really disappointed me. The costuming and the sets and the overall feel of the film were spot on which I feel like Sofia Coppola is really best at is creating an atmosphere. She’s truly an auteur. 

HOWEVER, I feel like the film felt a bit… Rushed and kind of missing some things for me. One of the biggest things that I really think she left out and was a huge problem for me as a film was the complete lack of using the house as a metaphor for the degradation of the mental health of the sisters, as well as a metaphor for the lack of care and neglect from the parents. In the novel, the house is an important part of the book. It’s kind of like a character in itself, and that it communicates where we are mentally through throughout the entire book.  The worst the situation at home gets and the more the girls are imprisoned inside the more the house itself is neglected like it’s filthy. It’s dirty. They are molding sandwiches on the staircases and it hasn’t been cleaned and it’s getting broken down. It’s such an important visual metaphor, and the fact that it wasn’t included in the film as much as it should’ve been to me took away most of what made that book so impactful.

And I’m not really sure why it wasn’t put in there because that would’ve been a really really easy thing to translate to film to communicate what’s going on without needing voiceover or anything. I couldn’t really get past that because I just feel like it was such a loss opportunity. I also didn’t really like the casting of the mother. I feel like the film made her look a bit more messy and in the book she seems really put together and stern and cold and I just don’t get that from the actress that played her in the film.

The girls were perfect though, and the guys were pretty good too.  I just found that the film lost a lot of meaning.
  - I missed the house as a metaphor as well. I think that also reinforces the idea that nobody saw those girls. Nobody heard them or paid attention. When they finally got to go out, the boys were stunned because they had different personalities and distinct ideas. Nobody saw the house either. The parents were bereft and just couldn’t or wouldn’t  function. 
    - Agreed it was such a powerful metaphor. I don’t really feel like you can tell the story properly without it.

## 2. Dial M for murder (1954) opinions?

**Score:** 0
**Body:** I'm honestly so confused by this movie. Margot (Grace Kelly) gets sentenced by a court and, on the day before her execution, the lead inspector, Mr. Combing-Mustache, starts a whole new investigation? What about due process?

Apparently, Hitchcock admitted that Dial M for Murder (1954) was routine work, shot in just 36 days to fulfill his studio contract. But the trope of the "perfect murder," which he explored in Rope (1948), seems to return here as a farce and maybe an ironic comment on the genre.

Many elements seem hilariously improbable. It starts with physical absurdities: Grace Kelly is being strangled, stabs her attacker in the back with a pair of scissors just once, and somehow he falls backward onto the scissors and dies? Haha.

Then we have the genius inspector, who initially investigates Grace Kelly and only after the court has sentenced her to death and any appeal is too late decides at the very last second to investigate the husband instead??? All of this makes very little sense from a legal perspective, unless you understand it as Hitchcock mocking the genre itself.

The bourgeois male obsession with the perfect crime could be seen as the true subject of the film. In Rear Window (1954), released that same year, Grace Kelly still possessed agency within the patriarchal order. Here, however, she is reduced to a passive object operating between four men who are all obsessed with crime:

Her husband (Tony): Who has been planning her murder ever since he discovered her affair.

The fraudster (Swann): Whom the husband blackmails into becoming a hitman.

The American boyfriend (Mark): A crime novelist who explains how he gets into the mind of a murderer.

The Inspector (Hubbard): A relic from a bygone era who represents the authority of the patriarchal order.

When viewed through these four vectors, a homosocial and latently homoerotic scene emerges, much like in Rope.

By committing adultery, the boyfriend effectively emasculates the husband. While the film highlights money as the central motive, we could also see the husband's humiliation and loss of control over the woman, the central prize of the patriarchal order, as a motive.

The husband uses another man to commit his murder for him: a former college acquaintance who has fallen from upper-class grace and now survives as a small-time con artist. The husband seems to derive a distinct sadistic pleasure from laying bare his peer's downfall and forcing him into committing murder.

The wounded male ego takes revenge not only on the woman, but on another, socially weaker man, reclaiming a sense of lost masculinity through his domination of him. In modern terms, the boyfriend made a cuckold out of the husband, so the husband seeks out a subordinate man to perform a surrogate act of domination.

Into this chaos of patriarchal vectors steps the Inspector. He initially subjects the woman to the doom of the judicial system, only to play the all-knowing savior outside of due process. He acts as the protective father figure and deus ex machina.

Just like Rope, Dial M for Murder deconstructs bourgeois-patriarchal civility. But while Rupert in Rope experiences a genuine catharsis, Inspector Hubbard feels more like a farce. In the face of upper-class horrors, at least we can still rely on the man with the well-combed mustache. But what when he is gone?

### Top 1 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. This film was shot in 3D, much to the disdain of Hitch, but I enjoy viewing it as such. Movie goers weren't keen on 3D, and soon the film was screened flat, and they came in drives to see it.

From Wikipedia:

According to his biographer, Donald Spoto, Hitchcock was not enthusiastic about the film, and Spoto quotes Grace Kelly to the effect that "the only reason [Hitchcock] could remain calm was that he was already preparing his next picture, 
Rear Window
".

Both the screenplay and the successful stage play on which it was based were written by English playwright 
Frederick Knott
. The play premiered in 1952 on 
BBC Television
,
 
before being performed on stage in the same year in London's 
West End
 in June, and then New York City's 
Broadway
 in October.

Reception:

Bosley Crowther of 
The New York Times described the film as a "technical triumph" for Hitchcock, in a favourable review. "It is one for which he needed good actors. He has them—and the best of the lot is John Williams, late of the stage play, who is the detective who solves the sinister ruse." 

Variety wrote: "There are a number of basic weaknesses in the set-up that keep the picture from being a good suspense show for any but the most gullible. Via the performances and several suspense tricks expected of Hitchcock, the weaknesses are glossed over to some extent, but not enough to rate the film a cinch winner." 

Harrison's Reports wrote that the film "shapes up as no more than a mild entertainment, despite the expert direction of Hitchcock and the competent acting of the players. The chief weakness is that the action is slow, caused by the fact that the story unfolds almost entirely by dialogue."

Richard L. Coe of 
The Washington Post called the film "completely choice", with Williams and Dawson "smooth as silk in reprising their stage roles", adding, "Hitch has a field day with his camera angles, darting our eyes now here, now there, doing tingling tricks with shadows and long longshots in quick contrast to fuzzed close-ups. It's the work of a master enjoying his script." 

John McCarten of 
The New Yorker wrote a generally positive review, writing that he wished the script would have given Hitchcock "a chance to cut loose with one of those spectacular chases he used to specialize in", but finding that after a talky opening 30 minutes, "things speed up once the murder wheels are set in motion, and eventually the piece becomes grimly diverting".

The Monthly Film Bulletin wrote that the film "offers the prolific Hitchcock little more than an opportunity to carpenter a neat piece of filmed theatre—an opportunity which perhaps satisfied the master a little more than it does us ... The characters are fitted to their situations, and hardly exist in themselves (nor are they enlivened by the rather drab performances of Ray Milland, Grace Kelly, and Robert Cummings); only John Williams' dry, sardonic police inspector has a touch of individuality."
